voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Energy applications: springs, power and collisions

sources.title: NCERT Physics: Work, Energy and Power

chapters.title: Variable force: count the signed area
chapters.formula: W = integral F(x) dx; W_net = delta K
points: Area under a force-position graph gives work, not impulse.
For F = 2x + 2 N from x = 0 to 3 m: W = 15 J.
A 2 kg particle starting from rest reaches sqrt(15) m/s if this is the net work.
chapters.script: Welcome back. Today we turn our energy basics into a practical problem solving toolkit. We will connect changing forces, springs and collisions, and learn when energy needs a second equation to help it. Start with a force that changes with position. Over a tiny displacement, the work is the force component along the motion times that displacement. Adding these little contributions gives an integral. On a force versus position graph, work is the signed area under the curve. Do not confuse it with a force versus time graph, whose area gives impulse. Let the net force along a straight line be two x plus two newtons, where x is measured in meters. A two kilogram particle starts from rest at x equal to zero and reaches x equal to three. The force rises from two to eight newtons. Predict the work before doing calculus. The graph is a trapezoid, so its area is the average of two and eight, multiplied by three. That gives fifteen joules. Integrating gives x squared plus two x, evaluated from zero to three: nine plus six, again fifteen. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy. For our two kilogram particle, one half m v squared is simply v squared in SI units. The final speed is therefore the square root of fifteen meters per second. Negative areas subtract work; they do not become positive because we call them areas. If the plotted force is only one of several forces, add the work of the others before applying the theorem. Check the horizontal axis first: position gives energy, time gives momentum change.

chapters.title: Power tells us how fast energy transfers
chapters.formula: P = F dot v; average P = W / delta t
points: Instantaneous power uses force and velocity at the same instant.
A 4 kg load lifted at constant 2 m/s with g = 10 needs 80 W mechanical power.
Efficiency relates useful output power to input power.
chapters.script: Two motors can do the same work, yet finish at different times. Power measures the rate of energy transfer. Average power is work divided by the time interval. Instantaneous power is the dot product of force and velocity. In words, take the component of force along the velocity and multiply by speed. Why the dot product? Work already counts the force component along displacement. Dividing a tiny amount of work by its tiny time interval replaces displacement by velocity. Imagine lifting a four kilogram load vertically at a steady two meters per second. Use g equal to ten and neglect other resistance. Steady velocity means zero acceleration, so the upward lifting force is forty newtons. Its mechanical power is forty times two, or eighty watts. Gravity's power is minus eighty watts. The net power is zero, consistent with unchanged kinetic energy, while gravitational potential energy increases. This is a nice reminder: zero net work on a particle does not mean the motor does no work. Suppose the motor is eighty percent efficient. What electrical input power is needed for this eighty watt useful output? Think about which number should be larger. Efficiency is useful output divided by input. Input is eighty divided by zero point eight, or one hundred watts. If a pulling force stays fixed while speed doubles along the same direction, its instantaneous power doubles. If supplied power is fixed instead, the available force is power divided by speed for collinear motion. Use this only where the constant power model applies; it does not predict a realistic infinite force at zero speed.

chapters.title: A spring stores energy gradually
points: The spring force opposes displacement from its natural length.
k = 200 N/m and compression 0.20 m store 4 J.
A 2 kg block released on a smooth horizontal surface reaches 2 m/s at natural length.
chapters.script: A spring becomes harder to stretch as its deformation grows. For an ideal spring within its linear elastic range, its force on the attached block is minus k x. Here x is the signed displacement from the spring's natural length, and k is its stiffness. The minus sign says the spring force points back toward natural length. To store energy slowly, an external agent must oppose that changing force. The force versus extension graph is a triangle. Its area gives one half k x squared, the elastic potential energy. Compression stores energy too because x is squared. Take a two kilogram block attached to a light spring on a smooth horizontal surface. The stiffness is two hundred newtons per meter. Compress the spring by zero point two meters and release the block from rest. The stored energy is one half times two hundred times zero point two squared, or four joules. At natural length the spring energy is zero. With no dissipative work, those four joules become kinetic energy. One half times two times v squared equals four, so the speed is two meters per second. Now add a rough region that removes one joule before the block reaches natural length. What changes? Pause. Only three joules remain as kinetic energy, so the speed becomes the square root of three meters per second. Do not call energy destroyed: it has transferred into internal energy of the contacting materials. For this chosen system, initial mechanical energy plus nonconservative work equals final mechanical energy. State which forces are represented by potential energy so you do not count their work twice.

chapters.title: A vertical circle needs energy and force
chapters.formula: String at top: T + mg = mv_top^2/r; v_bottom,min = sqrt(5gr)
points: A light string can pull but cannot push.
At the marginal top condition T = 0 and v_top^2 = gr.
Smooth motion from bottom to top gains height 2r; use energy as well as the radial equation.
chapters.script: Here is a problem where energy alone is not enough. A small particle on a light inextensible string moves in a vertical circle. Gravity is uniform and we neglect drag. The string must remain taut, and a string can pull but cannot push. At the top, inward means downward. Both weight and tension point inward, so T plus m g equals m v top squared divided by r. The smallest possible top speed for the marginal taut condition has tension equal to zero. That gives v top squared equal to g r. A slightly larger speed gives positive tension. Now connect bottom and top using energy. The particle rises by two r, and ideal tension does no work because it is perpendicular to the motion. The decrease in kinetic energy equals m g times two r. Therefore v bottom squared equals v top squared plus four g r. Substitute the limiting top value and obtain five g r. The minimum bottom speed is the square root of five g r for this ideal string model. Try r equal to two meters and g equal to ten. The minimum bottom speed is ten meters per second, while the top speed is the square root of twenty. For a one kilogram particle at the bottom, inward is upward: T minus ten equals one times one hundred divided by two. Bottom tension is sixty newtons. That tension is not forty; remember to include weight in the force balance. A rigid rod or a particle constrained on a track has different contact conditions, so do not transfer the string result automatically. In JEE, energy connects speeds at different heights, while the radial force equation checks whether the assumed motion is physically allowed.

chapters.title: Collisions: momentum first, energy second
chapters.formula: p_before = p_after if external impulse is negligible; elastic: K_before = K_after
points: Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.
A 2 kg body at 6 m/s hitting a stationary 1 kg body elastically gives velocities 2 and 8 m/s.
If they stick instead, common velocity = 4 m/s and kinetic energy decreases by 12 J.
chapters.script: For a collision, begin by choosing both bodies as your system. During the short interaction, neglect net external impulse when the stated conditions justify it. Then total momentum is conserved. This does not automatically conserve kinetic energy. In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved. In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and share a final velocity. Let a two kilogram body moving right at six meters per second hit a stationary one kilogram body in a one dimensional elastic collision. Initial momentum is twelve kilogram meters per second, and kinetic energy is thirty six joules. The elastic separation speed equals the approach speed. So v two minus v one equals six, while momentum gives two v one plus v two equals twelve. Substitute v two equal to v one plus six. Three v one equals six, giving v one equal to two and v two equal to eight meters per second. Check the energy: the two kilogram body has four joules and the one kilogram body has thirty two. Total, thirty six. Now let the same bodies stick together instead. Momentum gives three times their common velocity equal to twelve, so the velocity is four. Final kinetic energy is one half times three times sixteen, or twenty four joules. The twelve joule decrease becomes other forms of energy; total energy has not vanished. Momentum is a signed equation, whereas kinetic energy uses speed squared. These examples assume translational particle motion without rotation. Do not impose both sticking and elastic kinetic energy conservation on a moving collision: those are different models.

chapters.title: Two dimensions: conserve each momentum component
chapters.formula: Sum px before = Sum px after; Sum py before = Sum py after
points: For sticking masses 2 kg at 3 m/s east and 1 kg at 6 m/s north: v = (2, 2) m/s.
Final speed is 2 sqrt(2) m/s; translational kinetic energy decreases from 27 to 12 J.
Elastic scattering needs component momentum equations and kinetic energy, plus enough directional information.
chapters.script: Momentum conservation is a vector statement, so a collision does not have to stay on one line. Take a two kilogram particle traveling east at three meters per second and a one kilogram particle traveling north at six meters per second. They stick together; external impulse is negligible, and treat the combined object as a particle with no rotational energy. Choose east as positive x and north as positive y. Initial x momentum is six, and initial y momentum is also six. The combined mass is three kilograms. Divide each component by three, giving a final velocity of two east and two north, in meters per second. The speed is the square root of two squared plus two squared, or two times the square root of two. The direction is forty five degrees north of east. Why not add three and six to get nine? Because the initial velocities belong to different masses and different directions. Add momentum components, not speed magnitudes. Initial kinetic energy is nine plus eighteen, or twenty seven joules. Final kinetic energy is one half times three times eight, or twelve joules. Fifteen joules have left translational kinetic energy. Now consider equal masses in an elastic scattering example. One starts at ten meters per second east; the other is stationary. Possible final velocities are five east plus five north, and five east plus five south. Their vector sum preserves momentum, and their equal speeds of five times square root of two preserve the initial fifty joules for one kilogram masses. The final velocity vectors are perpendicular. This special result excludes a zero final velocity and assumes an initially stationary equal mass target. General two dimensional scattering needs enough angle or interaction information to determine a unique outcome. Use the practice questions to test the model before trusting a memorized formula.

quiz.question: The net force is F = 2x + 2 N along x, with x in meters. Work from x = 0 to 3 m is:
A motor lifts 4 kg at constant 2 m/s; g = 10 m/s^2, with no other resistance. At 80% efficiency its input power is:
quiz.explanation: Useful power = mgv = 80 W. Input = output/efficiency = 80/0.8 = 100 W.

quiz.question: An ideal spring of k = 200 N/m compressed 0.20 m releases a 2 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface. Speed at natural length is:
A 1 kg particle just completes a vertical circle on a light string, r = 2 m and g = 10 m/s^2. At the bottom its tension is:
quiz.explanation: Minimum bottom v^2 = 5gr = 100. T - mg = mv^2/r = 50, so T = 60 N.

quiz.question: A 2 kg particle at +6 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg particle in a 1D elastic collision with negligible external impulse. Their final velocities are:
quiz.explanation: 2v1 + v2 = 12 and v2 - v1 = 6 give v1 = 2, v2 = 8. Kinetic energy also remains 36 J.

quiz.question: If the same 2 kg and 1 kg particles stick instead, the decrease in translational kinetic energy is:
quiz.explanation: Common speed = 12/3 = 4 m/s. Initial K = 36 J, final K = (1/2)3(4)^2 = 24 J, decrease = 12 J.

quiz.question: Particles of 2 kg at 3 m/s east and 1 kg at 6 m/s north stick in the particle model, with negligible external impulse. Final speed is:
quiz.explanation: Momentum components are (6,6) kg m/s. Divide by 3 kg to obtain velocity (2,2) m/s, with magnitude 2 sqrt(2).

quiz.question: In that perpendicular sticking collision, the decrease in translational kinetic energy is:
